items.title: Attacker Eyes
items.question: A security review asks how the system could be breached rather than only how it will be used. What does this stance reveal?
choices: An attacker finds the gap you ignored
items.correctAnswer: An attacker finds the gap you ignored
items.correctExplanation: Right. Adopting a hostile viewpoint surfaces weaknesses that a friendly perspective overlooks.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is an attacker finds the gap you ignored. Thinking adversarially exposes assumptions that ordinary use never tests.
items.lessonContent:
Hostile viewpoints reveal hidden weaknesses.
Designers share blind spots with users.
Attack the design before others do.
Adopt the opponent's eyes.
Share this: find one weak point in a plan by asking how to break it.

items.title: Opposing Case
items.question: A team appoints someone to argue rigorously against its own proposal. What is this practice called?
choices: Red teaming argues the opposing case
items.correctAnswer: Red teaming argues the opposing case
items.correctExplanation: Right. Deliberately assigning the opposition tests the plan before reality does.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is red teaming argues the opposing case. The role is serious argument, not token dissent or mere brainstorming.
items.lessonContent:
Assigning opposition tests a plan.
Serious dissent beats polite agreement.
Weaknesses found early are cheap.
Make criticism a role, not a risk.
Share this: argue against one of your own decisions this week.

items.title: Strongest Version
items.question: Before responding to an argument, you restate it in its most defensible form. What is this called?
items.correctAnswer: Steelmanning strengthens the other side
items.correctExplanation: Right. Answering the best version of a view avoids the easy victory of a distorted target.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is steelmanning strengthens the other side. It is the opposite of attacking a weakened caricature.
items.lessonContent:
Answer the best version of a view.
Defeating a weak version proves little.
Strengthen before you critique.
Understand fully, then respond.
Share this: restate an opposing view better than its holder did.

items.title: Role Not Belief
items.question: Someone argues a position they do not hold in order to test a discussion. What role are they playing?
choices: A devil's advocate tests an idea
items.correctAnswer: A devil's advocate tests an idea
items.correctExplanation: Right. The role exists to stress-test reasoning, not to declare a personal view.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is a devil's advocate tests an idea. Their argument is a probe, so the position need not reflect their belief.
items.lessonContent:
Roles can be played for a purpose.
Test ideas from an uncommitted angle.
Separate the role from the person.
Value the probe, not the pose.
Share this: play the sceptic on one plan you actually like.

items.title: Binding Future
items.question: A person locks away tempting food to protect their later choices. What strategy is this?
items.correctAnswer: Precommitment binds your future self
items.correctExplanation: Right. Acting now to constrain later options guards against predictable weakness.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is precommitment binds your future self. It assumes your future self will be tempted and removes the choice in advance.
items.lessonContent:
Present action can constrain later choices.
Anticipate your own weakness.
Design the environment before temptation.
Make the good choice the easy one.
Share this: set up one constraint against a known weak moment.

items.title: Moving Target
items.question: Why does a fixed defence eventually fail against a determined opponent?
items.correctAnswer: Adversaries adapt to your defences
items.correctExplanation: Right. Any static arrangement can be studied and worked around by someone with the will to try.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is adversaries adapt to your defences. The assumption of a static opponent is what makes a plan fragile.
items.lessonContent:
Opponents react to what you do.
Static plans invite circumvention.
Assume adaptation on the other side.
Review and revise defences.
Share this: identify one plan that assumes the other side stays still.

items.title: Misuse First
items.question: A designer lists how a feature might be misused before listing its intended uses. What are they mapping?
choices: Enumerate abuse cases not just uses
Design only for the happy path
items.correctAnswer: Enumerate abuse cases not just uses
items.correctExplanation: Right. Anticipating misuse shapes a design that survives hostile or careless behaviour.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is enumerate abuse cases not just uses. The happy path is not the only path, and the others need design too.
items.lessonContent:
Design for misuse, not only use.
Hostile behaviour follows different incentives.
Anticipate the unintended path.
Test the edges, not just the centre.
Share this: list three ways one of your plans could be misused.

items.title: Proving Wrong
items.question: A scientist devises an experiment that could disprove their favourite theory. What principle is at work?
choices: Seek what would prove you wrong
items.correctAnswer: Seek what would prove you wrong
items.correctExplanation: Right. A claim earns confidence by surviving genuine attempts to refute it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is seek what would prove you wrong. Looking only for support produces comfort, not knowledge.
items.lessonContent:
Confidence grows by surviving refutation.
Design tests that could fail.
Confirmation alone proves little.
Prefer the risky test.
Share this: name one result that would change your mind about a belief.

items.title: Reading Motives
items.question: Rather than listening to a party's stated goals, an analyst studies what they stand to gain. Why?
choices: Read others incentives not their words
items.correctAnswer: Read others incentives not their words
items.correctExplanation: Right. Incentives predict behaviour more reliably than announcements, which can be strategic.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is read others incentives not their words. What a party gains shapes what they will actually do, spoken aims notwithstanding.
items.lessonContent:
Incentives predict behaviour well.
Statements can be strategic.
Look past the announcement.
Predict action from advantage.
Share this: predict one person's next move from what they gain.

items.title: Finding the Motive
items.question: An investigator traces who profits from a decision in order to understand why it was made. What are they doing?
choices: Follow the incentives to find the motive
items.correctAnswer: Follow the incentives to find the motive
items.correctExplanation: Right. Benefits reveal likely motivations that public reasons may leave out.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is follow the incentives to find the motive. Understanding who gains clarifies puzzling choices.
items.lessonContent:
Benefits hint at reasons.
Ask who gains from a decision.
Motives can differ from explanations.
Trace the advantage.
Share this: ask who benefits from one decision you recently heard about.

items.title: Who Pays
items.question: Before trusting a study, a reader checks who funded it and what the funder wants. Which safeguard is this?
items.correctAnswer: Check for conflicts of interest
items.correctExplanation: Right. Interests can shape questions, methods, and reporting even without deliberate dishonesty.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is check for conflicts of interest. Funding does not prove bias but it is a relevant condition to weigh.
items.lessonContent:
Interests can shape what is studied and shown.
Funding is relevant, not decisive.
Weigh the source before the claim.
Ask who benefits from the result.
Share this: check the funding behind one claim you trust.

items.title: After the Reaction
items.question: A policy will change behaviour in ways the designer did not intend. What must be considered?
items.correctAnswer: Second-order effects change the outcome
items.correctExplanation: Right. Following the consequences of responses reveals effects that a static analysis misses.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is second-order effects change the outcome. People adapt to new rules, so the world after the change differs from the world used to design it.
items.lessonContent:
Interventions trigger reactions.
Follow effects past the first step.
People adapt to new rules.
Model responses, not just actions.
Share this: trace one decision two steps past its first result.

items.title: Floor of Readiness
items.question: A planner prepares for the worst plausible case rather than the average. What does this establish?
choices: Worst-case analysis sets a readiness floor
No preparation is needed at all
items.correctAnswer: Worst-case analysis sets a readiness floor
items.correctExplanation: Right. Preparing for the extreme guarantees a minimum capability even though the event itself remains uncertain.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is worst-case analysis sets a readiness floor. It does not forecast one scenario but ensures a baseline response.
items.lessonContent:
Preparedness is measured against the extreme.
A floor beats a forecast.
Define the minimum acceptable response.
Check feasibility before committing.
Share this: set a minimum standard for handling one worst case.

items.title: Surface the Hidden
items.question: Before committing to a plan, a team writes out what must be true for it to succeed. What is this exercise?
items.correctAnswer: Surface assumptions before committing
items.correctExplanation: Right. Naming the beliefs a plan depends on turns hidden risks into testable claims.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is surface assumptions before committing. Unstated beliefs are the ones that quietly sink a plan.
items.lessonContent:
Hidden beliefs cause quiet failures.
Write out what must hold true.
Test assumptions before they matter.
Make the implicit explicit.
Share this: list three assumptions behind one plan you hold.

items.title: Both Chairs
items.question: A debater argues first for a proposal and then against it with equal effort. What does this accomplish?
choices: Playing both sides exposes weak points
It wastes time with no benefit
It proves the proposal is correct
items.correctAnswer: Playing both sides exposes weak points
items.correctExplanation: Right. Switching sides forces a fair hearing of both cases and reveals where each is vulnerable.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is playing both sides exposes weak points. Arguing each position seriously deepens understanding of the whole issue.
items.lessonContent:
Arguing both ways deepens understanding.
Each side reveals the other's gaps.
Sympathy for both sharpens judgement.
Rotate perspectives deliberately.
Share this: argue an issue first one way, then the other.

items.title: Hostile User
items.question: An engineer asks how a determined bad actor would misuse a new feature. What question are they answering?
choices: Ask what a hostile user would exploit
Ask what a friendly user prefers
Ask what looks best in a demo
items.correctAnswer: Ask what a hostile user would exploit
items.correctExplanation: Right. Imagining the worst user turns design flaws into concrete attack paths before they are used.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is ask what a hostile user would exploit. Friendly use cases rarely reveal what a malicious one would find.
items.lessonContent:
Imagine the worst user.
Hostile use reveals design gaps.
Friendly cases hide attack paths.
Design for the adversary.
Share this: ask how one tool could be used to cause harm.

items.title: Two Kinds Unknown
items.question: Why should a decision distinguish outcomes with known odds from outcomes with unknown odds?
choices: The two are exactly the same
items.correctAnswer: Distinguish risk from uncertainty
items.correctExplanation: Right. Risks can be priced and hedged, while true uncertainty cannot be reduced to a reliable number.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is distinguish risk from uncertainty. Treating the unknown as if it had known odds creates false confidence.
items.lessonContent:
Some unknowns have odds; others do not.
Do not assign numbers without a basis.
Handle uncertainty differently from risk.
Name which kind you face.
Share this: label one current unknown as risk or uncertainty.

items.title: One Weak Link
items.question: A chain of safeguards fails because a single element is missing. What concept does this illustrate?
choices: Find the single point of failure
items.correctAnswer: Find the single point of failure
items.correctExplanation: Right. Identifying the one element whose loss breaks everything guides where to add protection.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is find the single point of failure. Systems often have one vulnerable link that determines overall reliability.
items.lessonContent:
Reliability can hinge on one link.
Map which losses are fatal.
Protect the critical element.
Redundancy helps where it matters.
Share this: name the single element whose loss would break one system you rely on.

items.title: Survive Being Wrong
items.question: Why does an investor spread holdings across different assets?
choices: Keep all eggs in one basket
items.correctAnswer: Diversify to survive being wrong
items.correctExplanation: Right. Spreading exposure limits the damage any single mistake can cause.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is diversify to survive being wrong. Accepting that predictions fail, the strategy reduces the cost of being mistaken.
items.lessonContent:
Assume some predictions will fail.
Spread exposure to limit damage.
Diversification manages error.
Design for survival, not just success.
Share this: find one plan that survives a wrong prediction.

items.title: Fighting Bias
items.question: A writer actively searches for evidence against their own position. What error are they guarding against?
choices: Seek disconfirmation of your own view
items.correctAnswer: Seek disconfirmation of your own view
items.correctExplanation: Right. Hunting for contrary evidence counters the tendency to notice only what confirms us.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is seek disconfirmation of your own view. Motivated reasoning fades when you actively look for counterevidence.
items.lessonContent:
We notice what confirms us.
Actively hunt for contrary evidence.
Comfortable beliefs need the most testing.
Seek the awkward fact.
Share this: read one source that disagrees with a view you hold.

items.title: Unlikely Failure
items.question: Why should a plan account for the failure mode that seems least likely?
choices: Plan for the failure you least expect
Assume the worst case cannot happen
items.correctAnswer: Plan for the failure you least expect
items.correctExplanation: Right. Overlooked failures often cause the most damage precisely because nobody prepared for them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is plan for the failure you least expect. Rare events can be catastrophic when no response exists.
items.lessonContent:
Overlooked failures hurt most.
Rare does not mean harmless.
Prepare a response before you need it.
Attend to the neglected case.
Share this: name one unlikely failure worthy of a contingency.

items.title: Check Separately
items.question: A buyer checks a claim with a second source that has no relationship to the first. Why?
items.correctAnswer: Verify claims independently
items.correctExplanation: Right. Independent confirmation is worth far more than repetition from parties who share the same origin.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is verify claims independently. Corroboration from a linked source is not real corroboration at all.
items.lessonContent:
Linked sources share the same errors.
Independence gives real confirmation.
Check whether sources are truly separate.
Test claims at the origin.
Share this: confirm one claim using a source that is not connected to the first.

items.title: Rules Can Bend
items.question: Before adopting a rule, a designer asks how people might follow it literally to absurd ends. What are they testing?
choices: Consider how a rule can be gamed
Assume rules are always followed in spirit
Trust that wording cannot be twisted
items.correctAnswer: Consider how a rule can be gamed
items.correctExplanation: Right. People optimise for the letter of a rule, so loopholes must be anticipated.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is consider how a rule can be gamed. Literal compliance can defeat the purpose the rule was written to serve.
items.lessonContent:
People optimise for the letter.
Wording creates loopholes.
Anticipate literal compliance.
Test a rule against its own purpose.
Share this: find one loophole in a rule you follow.

items.title: Competence Assumed
items.question: A strategist plans on the assumption that the opponent will act well, not badly. Why?
items.correctAnswer: Assume competence in your opponent
items.correctExplanation: Right. Plans that rely on the other side's mistakes are fragile, since good opponents will not make them.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is assume competence in your opponent. Preparing for a capable rival produces a plan that holds even when they play well.
items.lessonContent:
Do not rely on others' mistakes.
Assume a capable opponent.
Robust plans survive good play.
Prepare for the strong case.
Share this: revise one plan so it still works if others act well.

items.title: Review Beats Consensus
items.question: A team invites harsh critique before a launch rather than seeking quick agreement. What does this improve?
items.correctAnswer: Adversarial review beats optimistic consensus
items.correctExplanation: Right. Pressure-testing a plan uncovers problems that agreeable discussion would leave hidden.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is adversarial review beats optimistic consensus. Harmony feels good but it does not find the flaws that matter.
items.lessonContent:
Harmony can hide flaws.
Invite critique before the launch.
Reward the person who finds the problem.
Make dissent safe and early.
Share this: ask one person for harsh feedback on a plan this week.
